analysis.one_liner: Extends gun-sale background checks to gun shows, adds a waiting period for handguns, and restricts youth access to guns.
analysis.headline: This gun-violence bill drew 33 cosponsors in 1999 but was referred to House committees and subcommittees, never received a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have extended the Brady background check system to gun shows, required promoters to register and keep vendor records, imposed a 72-hour waiting period for handgun purchases, raised the minimum age for handgun sales to 21, required safety devices sold with every gun, limited handgun purchases to one per 30 days, banned imports of large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, tripled allowed inspections of gun dealers, and expanded prosecution and tracing programs [S2]. It was referred to the Judiciary and Ways and Means Committees in May 1999, then to subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities affected by gun violence, who would gain from universal background checks at gun shows, longer waiting periods, child-access penalties, and stronger penalties for gun traffickers [S2]. Federal, state, and local law enforcement would also gain funding and expanded crime-gun tracing programs [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill closes the 'gun show loophole' by making it unlawful for any non-licensed person to transfer a firearm at a gun show except through a licensed dealer who runs a Brady background check, and by requiring show promoters to register, verify vendor identities, and submit vendor ledgers to the Treasury [S2].

It imposes a mandatory 72-hour waiting period for handgun and semiautomatic assault weapon transfers and extends the background-check waiting window from three to five business days, giving law enforcement more time to complete checks [S2].

It bars sales of handguns, ammunition, semiautomatic assault weapons, and large-capacity magazines to anyone under 21, requires a secure storage device or safety device with every firearm sold by a dealer, and penalizes adults who knowingly allow a child access to a gun that causes death or serious injury [S2].

It limits handgun purchases to one per person per 30 days to combat trafficking, increases penalties for gun trafficking and recordkeeping offenses, bans importation of large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, and triples the allowed number of compliance inspections of firearms dealers to three per year [S2].

It authorizes funding for intensive firearms prosecution projects ($5 million for fiscal year 2000) and expands the Youth Crime Gun Interdiction Initiative to 75 city and county law enforcement agencies to trace the origins of recovered guns [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Gun dealers and manufacturers bear new compliance costs: mandatory safety devices with every sale, secure inventory storage, tripled inspections, monthly reports of secondhand guns, and license suspension or civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation [S2]. Gun show promoters and unlicensed sellers face registration fees, recordkeeping, and the loss of unchecked private sales [S2]. Law-abiding gun buyers face delays, the one-handgun-per-30-days limit, and adult gun owners face liability for child access [S2].

drawbacks.text: The one-handgun-per-30-days limit applies to every non-licensed buyer, restricting purchases by collectors, competitors, and people who legitimately want a second handgun, with only narrow exemptions such as immediate-family transfers, lost-gun replacements, and pawn redemptions [S2].

The bill authorizes the Treasury Secretary to enter gun show premises and examine dealer records and inventory without a showing of reasonable cause or a warrant, a search-power expansion gun owners would object to [S2].
The 72-hour handgun waiting period delays lawful purchases; the bill offers an exception only through a chief law enforcement officer's written statement that the buyer faces a threat to life [S2].

It treats expunged or set-aside juvenile adjudications as firearms prohibitions unless the state authority makes an individualized finding of public safety, a significant tightening of existing 'restoration of rights' rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit—closing the background-check gap at gun shows and adding waiting periods and trafficking penalties—directly targets how prohibited buyers obtain guns, and most of its provisions mirror rules that already apply at retail stores. The serious costs fall on gun businesses in compliance burdens and on some lawful buyers through the one-gun-per-month cap and longer waits. The juvenile-expungement provision is the most overreaching element, converting sealed juvenile records into lifetime gun prohibitions unless a state makes an individualized safety finding. On balance the consumer protections and enforcement tools outweigh the compliance costs, though the breadth of the one-gun rule drew fair criticism.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary and Ways and Means Committees in May 1999, the Judiciary Committee sent it to its Crime Subcommittee and Ways and Means sent it to its Trade Subcommittee, and neither advanced it; no vote ever happened before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the Youth Gun Crime Enforcement Act of 1999 on May 12, 1999, with more than two dozen original cosponsors listed in the introduction [S1].
The bill attracted 33 cosponsors in total, 32 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on May 12, 1999, with consideration split between committees for provisions in each one's jurisdiction [S5].

On May 21, 1999 it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, and on May 25, 1999 to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Trade; after that, no further action of any kind was taken [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun dealers, gun show promoters, and unlicensed private sellers, who are spared background-check, recordkeeping, storage, and inspection requirements. Nothing in the record shows an industry campaign, but the status quo these rules would have changed is what survived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers and gun show sellers

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: House Judiciary Committee member; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled more than two dozen original cosponsors at introduction [S3].

for.name: Rep. Constance Morella
for.role: Original cosponsor; one of two Republicans listed at introduction
for.what_they_did: Joined Conyers as an original cosponsor, the only Republican among the 33 total cosponsors [S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 12, 1999 and referred it to the Subcommittee on Crime on May 21, 1999; it never held a markup or reported the bill, and no vote ever occurred [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for its provisions within its jurisdiction and referred it to the Subcommittee on Trade on May 25, 1999; it never acted further [S5].

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.role: Gun-rights lobby opposing expanded gun regulation in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Opposed post-Columbine gun-control legislation and lobbied against expanded background checks and waiting periods during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 33 cosponsors, 32 were Democrats and 1 was a Republican; the record shows no floor vote, so the wider chambers' positions were never tested [S4].

industries.note: The bill requires safety devices with every sale, secure inventory storage, three compliance inspections per year instead of one, monthly reports of secondhand guns, and allows license suspension or $10,000-per-violation civil penalties. These compliance and enforcement costs are the price of the same rules that protect buyers [S2].

industries.industry: Gun show promoters and unlicensed private sellers
industries.note: Promoters would have to register with Treasury, pay a fee, verify vendor identities, and file vendor ledgers; all private sales at shows would have to run through a licensed dealer with a background check, ending the unchecked 'private seller' channel [S2].

The bill authorizes $5 million for intensive firearms prosecution projects and expands the Youth Crime Gun Interdiction Initiative to 75 city and county agencies with additional agents and analysts [S2].
